concepts.decision: Activate based on declared impact, recovery priorities, available strategy, authority, and safety conditions.
concepts.definition: The accountable process for restoring mission-critical technology and its dependencies after a disaster, within approved business recovery objectives.
concepts.failureExample: Treating DR as only backup restoration misses people, communications, dependencies, validation, and business acceptance.
concepts.label: Disaster Recovery Process

concepts.decision: Prioritize life safety and incident stabilization before recovery acceleration; coordinate with authorized responders.
concepts.definition: Immediate actions that protect life, stabilize the event, preserve essential evidence, and enable a safe handoff to assessment and recovery.
concepts.failureExample: Starting technical restoration while hazards or active compromise remain can harm people or destroy evidence.
concepts.label: Emergency Response

concepts.decision: Use current evidence to choose whether to recover in place, use an alternate capability, or escalate.
concepts.definition: The rapid assessment that determines affected scope, criticality, safety constraints, and feasible recovery options.
concepts.failureExample: Selecting a site or restore path before assessing dependencies can make the chosen plan impossible to execute.
concepts.label: Damage Assessment

concepts.decision: Select members and alternates for the services, facilities, suppliers, skills, and shifts actually in scope.
concepts.definition: The assigned technical and business participants who execute recovery tasks and communicate status under designated authority.
concepts.failureExample: A team with no business owner or dependency expertise may restore infrastructure without restoring the required service.
concepts.label: Recovery Team

concepts.decision: Choose based on recovery-time/data objectives, capacity, geographic and utility separation, security controls, and test evidence.
concepts.definition: A prearranged recovery location or capability selected to meet service objectives while avoiding the primary event’s correlated risks.
concepts.failureExample: A nearby or untested site can share the same disaster impact or fail to support required capacity and security.
concepts.label: Alternate Site

concepts.decision: Select based on recovery-point objective, restoration time, geographic/administrative separation, immutability or protection needs, and proven restore process.
concepts.definition: Protected recovery copies and their storage service, managed for recoverability, integrity, access control, retention, and required recovery point.
concepts.failureExample: A copy is not a recovery capability if it is inaccessible, corrupted, too old, compromised, or cannot be restored in time.
concepts.label: Backup Storage

concepts.decision: Transition when stable normal operations and all required acceptance evidence are available.
concepts.definition: A deliberate exit from recovery mode after validated service, reconciled data, accepted residual risk, communications, and documented closure.
concepts.failureExample: Switching back solely because systems are up can reintroduce unresolved defects or abandon temporary safeguards.
concepts.label: Return To Normal

concepts.decision: Use alternate channels, message ownership, approved facts, notification thresholds, and recorded decisions.
concepts.definition: Managed communications that provide accurate decisions, status, constraints, and instructions to each relevant audience throughout recovery.
concepts.failureExample: Uncoordinated updates can cause unsafe actions, duplicated work, misinformation, or regulatory/customer harm.
concepts.label: Recovery Communications

misconceptions.claim: The DR coordinator can make every business-priority decision.
misconceptions.correction: Business owners, technical leads, security, facilities, communications, legal, and executives each provide authority and acceptance for their decisions.

misconceptions.claim: A backup proves the service can be recovered.
misconceptions.correction: Recovery requires usable, trustworthy data, dependencies, access, keys, procedures, staff, capacity, and validation.

outcome: Given a disaster scenario, sequence the disaster-recovery process, identify the people and dependencies involved, preserve decision evidence, and coordinate recovery without treating restoration as the whole plan.

sections.body: A disaster-recovery process commonly includes activation criteria, emergency response and life safety, notification, assessment, stabilization, recovery operations, data and system restoration, validation, business acceptance, and return to normal. Assign roles and alternates, maintain contact information and dependencies, protect plan access, and make decisions traceable. A recovery team should know what it may do immediately and what requires escalation.
keyPoints: Life safety and emergency communications precede technology restoration.
Activation criteria and authority should be explicit before a crisis.
Dependencies include people, facilities, power, communications, suppliers, data, identity, and keys.
sections.title: Coordinate the process

sections.body: Recovery actions should use protected backups or alternate capabilities, verify system and data integrity, re-establish security controls, and monitor heightened risk. Business owners accept service against the recovery objectives and criteria; the team then manages backlog, communications, evidence, and return to normal or a sustained alternate mode. Record what worked, what failed, and which plan, contract, architecture, or training change is required.
keyPoints: A recovered system must be secure and usable, not merely powered on.
Business acceptance and security validation are distinct but coordinated decisions.
Return-to-normal can create another change and must be governed.
sections.title: Restore, validate, and transition

Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.
